units.title: Unit 1: Map Skills & Regions of the United States

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Latitude, Longitude, Map Tools & U.S. Regions
lessons.videoTitle: Geography Skills: Latitude, Longitude & Regions of the United States
lessons.reading: Geographers use a grid of imaginary lines to locate places on Earth. Lines of latitude (parallels) run east–west and measure distance north or south of the Equator (0° latitude). Lines of longitude (meridians) run north–south from pole to pole and measure distance east or west of the Prime Meridian. The United States is commonly grouped into five major regions: Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest, and West.

principles.title: Map Coordinates & Physical/Cultural Regions of the U.S.
principles.summary: Use latitude, longitude, compass rose, and map scales, and identify major landforms and U.S. regions.

bank.prompt: What is the imaginary line at 0° latitude that divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
bank.explanation: The Equator is 0° latitude, circling Earth halfway between the North and South Poles.

bank.prompt: Which tool on a map helps you convert inches or centimeters on the page into actual miles or kilometers on the ground?
bank.explanation: A map scale shows the ratio between distance on a map and real-world distance on Earth.

bank.prompt: Which U.S. region is famous for its fertile prairies and is often called "America’s Breadbasket" because of its corn and wheat farms?
bank.explanation: The flat, fertile plains of the Midwest make it one of the world’s most productive agricultural regions.

bank.prompt: Which major mountain range runs along the eastern United States from Maine to Georgia?
bank.explanation: The Appalachian Mountains are the ancient mountain chain in eastern North America.

bank.prompt: Lines of longitude run from the North Pole to the South Pole and measure distance east or west of the:
bank.explanation: The Prime Meridian (0° longitude) is the starting reference line for measuring east and west longitude.

bank.prompt: The Grand Canyon, Sonoran Desert, and Colorado Plateau are signature physical features of which U.S. region?
bank.explanation: Arid deserts, canyons, and mesas characterize the American Southwest (including Arizona and New Mexico).

bank.prompt: Which river system forms a massive north-to-south waterway through the center of the United States emptying into the Gulf of Mexico?
bank.explanation: The Mississippi River and its tributaries drain the interior of the United States into the Gulf of Mexico.

bank.prompt: What is the purpose of a map legend (or key)?
choices: To explain the meaning of symbols, colors, and lines used on the map
To show which direction is north
To list the authors of the atlas
bank.answer: To explain the meaning of symbols, colors, and lines used on the map
bank.explanation: A map legend decodes what the symbols and colors represent (e.g., capitals, highways, elevation).

units.title: Unit 2: U.S. Constitution, Branches of Government & Economics

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Three Branches of Government & Checks and Balances
lessons.videoTitle: The U.S. Constitution & Three Branches of Government
lessons.reading: The U.S. Constitution divides federal power among three branches so no single leader or group gains total control (Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances): 1) Legislative Branch (Congress: Senate and House of Representatives) makes laws; 2) Executive Branch (President, Vice President, Cabinet) carries out and enforces laws; 3) Judicial Branch (Supreme Court and federal courts) interprets laws under the Constitution.

principles.title: Legislative, Executive & Judicial Branches and Citizens’ Rights
principles.summary: Congress makes laws, the President enforces laws, and the Supreme Court interprets laws under Checks and Balances.

bank.prompt: Which branch of the U.S. government is responsible for MAKING federal laws?
bank.explanation: Congress—made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives—writes and votes on bills to make federal laws.

bank.prompt: Why did the framers of the Constitution create a system of "Checks and Balances"?
choices: To prevent any single branch of government from becoming too powerful
To help banks print paper money faster
To give the President complete power to write all laws alone
bank.answer: To prevent any single branch of government from becoming too powerful
bank.explanation: Checks and balances give each branch ways to limit the power of the other two branches.

bank.prompt: Who leads the Executive Branch of the federal government and serves as Commander-in-Chief?
choices: The President of the United States
bank.answer: The President of the United States
bank.explanation: The President heads the Executive Branch and sees that federal laws are faithfully executed.

bank.prompt: What are the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution called?
bank.explanation: Ratified in 1791, the Bill of Rights guarantees fundamental freedoms such as speech, religion, press, and fair trial.

bank.prompt: Which branch of government includes the Supreme Court and decides whether laws follow the Constitution?
bank.explanation: The Judicial Branch interprets laws and can strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

bank.prompt: When the President refuses to sign a bill passed by Congress, this action is called a:
bank.explanation: A presidential veto is an executive check on the legislative branch (which Congress can override with a two-thirds vote).

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, Supply & Demand
lessons.videoTitle: Economics: Goods, Services, Opportunity Cost & Supply/Demand
lessons.reading: Economics studies how people use limited resources to satisfy wants and needs. Scarcity means resources (time, money, raw materials) are limited. When you make a choice, your opportunity cost is the value of the NEXT BEST alternative you gave up. Supply is how much of a good producers offer for sale, and demand is how much consumers are willing and able to buy.

principles.title: Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, Goods/Services & Supply/Demand
principles.summary: Opportunity cost is the next best choice given up; high demand and low supply push prices up.

bank.prompt: Liam has $15. He wants either a board game or a soccer ball, and he chooses the soccer ball. What is his OPPORTUNITY COST?
choices: The board game he gave up
Both the board game and the soccer ball
bank.answer: The board game he gave up
bank.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative you give up when making a decision.

bank.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a SERVICE rather than a physical GOOD?
choices: A loaf of fresh bread from a bakery
bank.explanation: A service is helpful work performed for others, whereas a good is a physical object you can touch.

bank.prompt: If a late spring freeze destroys most of the peach crop while many shoppers still want peaches, what usually happens to the price of peaches?
choices: The price increases because supply is low and demand is high.
The supply of peaches doubles overnight.
Peaches become a free public service.
bank.answer: The price increases because supply is low and demand is high.
bank.explanation: When supply decreases while demand remains strong, scarcity pushes the market price up.

bank.prompt: What does the economic term SCARCITY mean?
choices: People have unlimited wants, but resources to fulfill them are limited.
Stores have too many items on sale.
Everyone has enough money to buy everything at once.
Only gold and diamonds have value.
bank.answer: People have unlimited wants, but resources to fulfill them are limited.
bank.explanation: Scarcity is the fundamental economic condition of limited resources relative to human wants.

bank.prompt: A bakery buys flour, ovens, and mixing bowls to make muffins. In economics, the ovens and mixing bowls are:
bank.explanation: Man-made tools, machines, and buildings used to produce other goods are capital resources.

bank.prompt: When a toy store has 200 winter sleds left over in April and very few customers want to buy them, the store will likely:
choices: Lower the price (put them on sale) to encourage demand
Triple the price of the sleds
bank.answer: Lower the price (put them on sale) to encourage demand
bank.explanation: High supply paired with low demand leads sellers to reduce prices to clear inventory.

lessons.title: Unit 2 Exam: Civics, Geography & Economics
lessons.reading: Review U.S. regions, the three branches of government, and economic principles for the Unit 2 Exam.

principles.title: Legislative, Executive & Judicial Branches and Citizens’ Rights
principles.summary: Understand separation of powers and constitutional rights.

bank.prompt: How many U.S. Senators represent each state in Congress?
choices: It depends on the state’s land area
bank.explanation: Every state has equal representation in the U.S. Senate with 2 Senators.

bank.prompt: Freedom of speech, freedom of the press, and freedom of religion are protected by which amendment?
bank.explanation: The First Amendment in the Bill of Rights protects religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition.

bank.prompt: Which level of government is primarily responsible for local fire departments, city parks, and public libraries?
bank.explanation: Local governments manage community services like fire protection, local roads, parks, and libraries.

principles.title: Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, Goods/Services & Supply/Demand
principles.summary: Apply opportunity cost and supply/demand reasoning.

bank.prompt: Maya spends Saturday afternoon studying for her science test instead of going to the movies. Going to the movies is her:
bank.explanation: The activity she gave up (going to the movies) is the opportunity cost of her choice to study.

bank.prompt: Trees, fresh water, fertile soil, and iron ore used to make products are examples of:
bank.explanation: Materials that come directly from nature without being made by humans are natural resources.

bank.prompt: A person who buys and uses goods and services is called a:
bank.explanation: Producers make goods or provide services; consumers purchase and use them.
